name: Abel
title: The First Martyr
summary: Abel was the second son of Adam and Eve, and the first according to the biblical account to be murdered – killed by his own brother Cain. As a shepherd, he brought an offering from the firstborn of his flock with their fat, and God looked with favor on his offering, unlike Cain's offering. Abel's righteousness and faith make him a key figure throughout Scripture: Jesus calls him 'the righteous Abel' (Matt 23:35) and points to him as the first in the line of righteous martyrs. The Letter to the Hebrews highlights him as an example of faith, one who still speaks through his faith even after death (Heb 11:4). His blood cried out from the ground for justice – a cry that in Christian theology points forward to Christ's blood, which speaks of grace and reconciliation.

keyEvents.title: Birth
keyEvents.description: Eve gave birth to Abel as her second son. He became a shepherd while his brother Cain became a farmer.

keyEvents.title: The Accepted Offering
keyEvents.description: Abel brought the firstborn of his flock along with their fat, and God looked with favor on his offering, but he did not look with favor on Cain's offering.

keyEvents.title: Killed by Cain
keyEvents.description: Cain became jealous and lured Abel out into the field where he killed him—the first murder in the biblical narrative.

keyEvents.title: The Blood Cries Out from the Ground
keyEvents.description: God confronted Cain and said that Abel's blood was crying out to him from the ground. Cain was cursed away from the soil that had opened its mouth to receive Abel's blood.

keyEvents.title: The Example of Faith
keyEvents.description: The Letter to the Hebrews highlights that by faith Abel offered a better sacrifice than Cain, and through this he received testimony that he was righteous. He still speaks through his faith, even though he is dead.

keyEvents.title: Righteous Abel
keyEvents.description: Jesus refers to Abel as 'righteous Abel' and places him as the first in the line of the righteous who were killed, from Abel to Zechariah son of Barachiah.

versions.summary: Abel was Adam and Eve's second son and the first person to die in history—killed by his own brother Cain. He was a shepherd and offered a sacrifice from the firstborn of his flock, which God looked upon with favor. The Letter to the Hebrews calls him a hero of faith who still speaks through his faith.
versions.title: The First Martyr
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The First Martyr' is theologically interesting, but the term 'martyr' implies dying for one's faith. Abel was killed out of jealousy, not because he refused to deny his faith. A more precise title could be 'The First Person Killed' or 'Adam and Eve's Second Son'. Nevertheless, 'The First Martyr' is an established tradition, and Jesus himself refers to Abel as the first righteous person who was killed (Matt 23:35), so the title can be defended.; [major] Abel had more roles than just 'martyr'. He was a shepherd (Gen 4:2), and he is an example of faith according to Hebrews 11:4. The roles should be expanded to include at least 'shepherd' and 'example of faith'.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could also mention that Jesus himself refers to Abel as 'righteous Abel' (Matt 23:35), which underscores his biblical significance.; [major] Abel's mother should be referred to with the lowercase id 'eva'. The Hebrew name is Havva/Eva. Check whether the id 'eva' matches the system's conventions – if the system uses 'havva' or similar, this should be updated. Here 'eva' is retained as it is most common in Norwegian.; [minor] It could have been useful to include Jesus' reference to Abel in Matt 23:35 as a key event, where Jesus calls him 'righteous Abel' and places him as the first in the line of righteous people who were killed.; [major] Footnotes are missing. A profile on Abel should include footnotes on, for example, the meaning of his name, the theology behind the offering, typological interpretation of Abel as a foreshadowing of Christ, and rabbinic interpretations of the Cain and Abel story.; [minor] The lifespan field is missing from the data. It should be set to a reasonable value, even though the Bible does not state Abel's exact age. A formulation such as 'Unknown' is appropriate.

footnotes.text: The name Abel (Hebrew: הֶבֶל, Hevel) means 'breath', 'vapor' or 'transient'. The name can be interpreted as a foreshadowing of his short life, or as a theological comment on the transience of life—the same word is used repeatedly in Ecclesiastes ('vanity' / 'transient').

Abel's offering of the firstborn from the flock with their fat (Gen 4:4) is considered by many theologians to be a precursor to the biblical principle of the firstfruits offering and blood sacrifice. Some see this as a typological pointer toward Christ as God's Lamb—the ultimate sacrificial gift.

In rabbinic tradition (Bereshit Rabba, Targum Pseudo-Jonathan) there are extensive discussions about what the conflict between Cain and Abel was really about. Some traditions claim they quarreled over the division of the world, over God's presence (Shekhina), or even over a woman. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 37b) uses Abel's blood (which is plural in Hebrew: 'your blood' = דָּמֶיךָ) to teach that killing one person is like killing an entire world.

Hebrews 11:4 says that Abel 'still speaks, even though he is dead'. Abel's blood cried out for justice from the ground (Gen 4:10), while Christ's blood according to Hebrews 12:4 'speaks more loudly than Abel's blood'—it speaks of grace and forgiveness rather than vengeance. Jesus refers to him as 'righteous Abel' (Matt 23:35) and places him as the first in the line of righteous martyrs, establishing Abel as a central figure in salvation history.

Archaeologically, the story of Cain and Abel reflects the early tension between nomadic shepherd culture and settled agricultural culture in the ancient Middle East. This conflict between herders and farmers is well documented in Sumerian and Mesopotamian sources, such as the story of Dumuzi (shepherd) and Enkimdu (farmer).
